content: Home cooking refers to the preparation of meals in one’s own residence using raw or minimally processed ingredients rather than eating commercially prepared foods. Mechanistically, cooking at home allows greater control over ingredient selection, portion sizes, and cooking methods, which can influence nutrient intake and reduce exposure to excess calories, unhealthy fats, salt, and added sugars. Home cooking can improve diet quality by increasing consumption of whole foods such as vegetables, fruits, legumes, and whole grains, which are often under-consumed in processed and fast foods. These dietary patterns are linked with decreased risk of chronic diseases including cardiovascular diseases, type 2 diabetes, and obesity. Major synonyms include “homemade meals,” “from-scratch cooking,” and “scratch cooking.” Limitations include time constraints, limited cooking skills, and accessibility to fresh ingredients, which can reduce cooking frequency or lead to unhealthy shortcuts. Safety considerations involve proper food handling, avoiding cross-contamination, and appropriate cooking temperatures to reduce risk of foodborne illness. Overall, home cooking represents a modifiable lifestyle behavior with substantial potential to improve nutritional health but requires education and practical strategies to overcome barriers and promote long-term adherence.
